stories.title: How will the State's savings and investment account work?
stories.summary: At the moment, most individuals leave money in deposit accounts in banks, which get negligible interest. The Government is working on a plan to encourage people to save for the future instead, by making it more attractive to consumers to put money into new investment accounts - which offer a better return. For example, while individuals are normally liable for tax on the interest earned on their savings, the new initiative would offer tax-free returns on investments up to a certain limit. So far, Minister for Finance Simon Harris has only announced the broad parameters of the scheme. The first returns from the account will be tax-free and - beyond that - a "low rate" of tax will apply, according to the Department of Finance. There will be no requirements to make a minimum contribution but an annual maximum limit will apply. The specific tax-free threshold, low tax rate and annual contribution will be announced as part of the Budget on 6 October.

stories.title: Calls for 'full cost review' into Govt's carbon tax plans
stories.summary: Fuels for Ireland has urged the Government not to "weaken" long-stated carbon tax plans without "a full cost review" of the potential measure. In recent days, the group has suggested that the Coalition could slow down the timing of planned carbon tax increases as part of October's budget. Under existing plans linked to climate action initiatives, the Government is due to increase carbon taxes resulting in a €53.50 rise in the price of home heating oil, a €4.86 rise in the price of a tank of petrol and a €5.76 rise in a tank of diesel by the end of the decade. However, with planned increases over summer being postponed due to Middle East war, it has been suggested further increases could also now be delayed. Responding to the rumours, Fuels for Ireland's Chief Executive Kevin McPartlan told the Government: "Carbon tax has a clear emissions-reduction purpose. Before Government changes its trajectory, it should examine the whole fuel-policy system, what each measure costs, what it delivers and how the measures interact. "If Government believes the total burden on motorists, businesses and households has become too high, it seems strange the next measure we might slow down is carbon tax without first examining everything else Government policy adds to the price of fuel.

stories.title: State lacks dedicated strategy for children in care
stories.summary: As Autumn approaches and the news cycle moves on, questions over the M9 crash will likely fade. Not so for the injured family and their loved ones, the tragedy of that Sunday morning is something they will have to endure for a lifetime. Five families who lost teenagers in the crash, including three members of the Traveller Community, will continue to process their loss. This week, Tánaiste Simon Harris described the issues raised by the crash as "deep-rooted" and "multifaceted", extending across social media, Government, the criminal justice system and road safety. No mention of the care system which formed part of three of the boys' lives; or the juvenile detention centre, Oberstown, which was familiar to one of the teenagers. On the same day he made his remarks, 17-year-old Jack Kennedy’s funeral was under way in Athy. It was the final funeral of the five.

stories.title: Sydney teacher hit shark with 'left hook' during attack
stories.summary: An Australian school teacher mauled by a large shark at a Sydney beach says she fired a "left hook" at the predator before it dragged her underwater. Leah Stewart, a primary school teacher, was placed in an induced coma and had part of her left arm amputated after the 13 June attack at Sydney's Coogee Beach. Ms Stewart decided to go for a late morning swim in the "crystal clear" sea, unknowingly sharing the water with a shark described by witnesses as a great white measuring up to four metres long. The teacher said she was finishing her swim and approaching the sand when she heard a girl scream. "I turned, and there was a huge, huge fin behind her. It was massive, and at first I thought, 'Oh, it's a dolphin'," she told Nine Network television's 60 Minutes programme. Ms Stewart added: "I looked at the size of it and I realised, that's not a dolphin. And so we just start screaming at the top of our lungs, just like 'shark, shark, shark'."

stories.title: Grehan believes conditions can give GB&I the edge
stories.summary: Stuart Grehan is hoping that some inclement weather on the west coast can give Great Britain and Ireland the edge in this weekend's Walker Cup. A sold out crowd of 16,000 fans will to descend on Lahinch Golf Club for the 51st staging of the Walker Cup as teams from Great Britain and Ireland and the United States go head-to-head. Great Britain and Ireland are seeking to win their first Walker Cup since 2015, when Nigel Edwards' side triumphed in Royal Lytham and St Anne's, with Paul Dunne, Gavin Moynihan, Gary Hurley and Jack Hume all featuring. The Clare links is the first Irish course to host the event since Royal County Down in 2007 and Grehan, who plays in his second successive Walker Cup, believes that both the course and the west of Ireland weather can give his team an edge. "I think we have a lot more experience than them on links golf. I would like a little bit of wind, I think we all would. "We're right on the Irish coast, the west coast here, so we're hoping there'll be a nice bit of breeze and maybe a bit of rain as well, just to kind of make it a bit advantageous for us.

stories.title: Ballygunner survive Fourmilewater scare to retain title
stories.summary: Ballygunner are kings of Waterford hurling for the 13th year running, but it was very much an unlucky 13 as they had to overcome a ferocious effort from rivals Fourmilewater to win out by four points at the finish. Trailing by three points with 53 minutes on the clock, the All-Ireland champions drew from every inch of their experience to outscore the Nire men 1-4 to nil down the home straight to march on to Munster once again - Mark Hartley's added-time goal ensuring another piece of silverware for Jason Ryan’s side. Playing in a 14th consecutive county decider, the Gunners arrived seeking a 13th News & Star Cup on the spin - facing a seventh different final opponent in the form of Fourmilewater, who themselves reached the last hurdle for the very first time in their 100-year history. Fourmilewater started the brighter, Sean Walsh getting out first to a breaking ball to split the posts with a minute played, but a great catch and score from Dessie Hutchinson soon drew the Gunners level. A superb effort on the left flank from Michael Morrissey was cancelled out by Conor Tobin, but Fourmilewater clicked into gear from here in what was a somewhat attritional beginning - bringing extreme physicality exemplified by Conor Gleeson, Dermot Ryan and Tholom Guiry. Liam O’Brien swivelled to restore the lead, before Jamie Barron got inside Philip Mahony and Paddy Leavey but his goal-bound strike could only find the side netting. Barron emerged from a ruck to split the posts, before Pauric Mahony opened his account at the other end - and Stephen Ryan had to be on hand to deny Kevin Mahony when sent racing through by Hutchinson.

stories.title: Hoops come from behind to salvage point in Derry
stories.summary: Two goals in eight second half minutes saw Shamrock Rovers come back from the dead to take a point at the Brandywell. Just days after exiting Europe, Rovers showed their fighting spirit yet again, with Stephen Bradley's second half substitutions - particularly William Fitzgerald and Dylan Watts - proving that they remain the standard in the league. It was at least a better showing from Mark Connolly's players than last week’s second half collapse against Bohemians, but City have now wasted half-time leads in their last two games, taking just one point in the process. The most notable chance from the City team which lost to Bohemians last week was in goal, as Reading loanee Tom Norcott came in for his debut in place of Brian Maher, who was only fit enough to make the substitutes’ bench. Derry City wasted no time in opening the scoring when Ellis Chapman won the ball from Lee Grace and immediately fed Michael Duffy, who raced into the area from the left and pulled it back for Chapman to sweep in his fourth goal for the club. The goal was timed at 81 seconds, City’s quickest goal of the season. The lead was doubled when John O’Sullivan lost possession too easily, eased off the ball 25 yards from goal by Chapman, and Darragh Burns took over, slipping the ball in behind for Duffy, who fired the ball past Ed McGinty for his fourth goal in three games.

stories.title: Buttimer strikes again as Munster retain Interpro title
stories.summary: Beth Buttimer haunted Leinster once again as Munster held off their rivals to retain their Vodafone Women's Interprovincial Championship at Dexcom Stadium. Three weeks on from scoring four tries in her side’s 39-19 win against the same opposition, Buttimer scored two more in today’s final in Galway to make it back-to-back Interpro championships for Matt Brown’s side. The hooker’s first score on 20 minutes had given her side a slender 7-5 lead at half time, with Kathy Baker crossing for Leinster shortly before the break. And it would take until the 70-minute mark for either team to add to their total, as Buttimer touched down from the back of a rolling maul, before Enya Breen landed a high-pressure conversion which put her side nine points ahead, and crucially give them a two-score buffer heading into the closing minutes. The afternoon may well have come at some cost for Ireland head coach Scott Bemand, who saw second row Ruth Campbell limp out of the Leinster side in the opening half. Three weeks out from his team’s opening WXV Global Series game against USA in Tallaght, the Ireland head coach will also have some important decisions to make.

stories.title: Star Trek at 60: its secret was exploring humanity, not aliens
stories.summary: When Star Trek first appeared on television screens 60 years ago, audiences expected science fiction to offer aliens, monsters and futuristic technology, writes Stephen McVeigh. From its very first broadcast episode on September 8 1966, Star Trek established that its true subject was the exploration of humanity itself. For all its reputation as an action-packed space adventure, the franchise has endured because it repeatedly returned to a universal question: what does it mean to be human? In that first episode, entitled The Man Trap, the alien antagonist survives by appearing to each observer as the person they most wish to see. Dr Leonard "Bones" McCoy meets a lost love from his past; others see figures shaped by memory, expectation, desire and longing. The creature, soon dubbed the "salt vampire" by fans of the series, is not simply a shape-shifter. Its power lies in exploiting human perception. Rather than asking viewers to fear an alien with superior strength or advanced weaponry, the episode asks a more profound question: can we trust our experience of reality? Watch a clip from The Man Trap, the first Star Trek episode to air in September 1966 Sixty years on, this question looks remarkably prescient. Modern neuroscience increasingly suggests that perception is not a passive recording of the external world. According to theories of predictive processing, the brain continually generates expectations and compares them with incoming sensory information.

stories.title: Dolly Parton's estate announces DollyFest to honour star
stories.summary: Dolly Parton's estate has announced that a two-day festival honouring the late singer will be held in Nashville and London. The country music singer died at the age of 80 on 25 August, following a "brief battle" with cancer. It has now been revealed that the two-day festival, Dollyfest, will be staged next year across two consecutive weekends. According to a press release, the festival was originally scheduled to take place in January 2026 – around Parton's 80th birthday – and was going to feature her as a performer and host. "We had the venue booked and we had the announcement ready to go. And then, in August 2025, Dolly had to take a step back after her initial health challenges," organiser Danny Nozell, Founder and Chief Executive of CTK Enterprises, said in a statement. "A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, Dollyfest is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!).

stories.title: Oran Aurelio on designing CMAT's Electric Picnic outfit
stories.summary: Charlotte Ryan speaks to Irish designer Oran Aurelio about creating CMAT's Electric Picnic outfit, evolving his iconic looks for The Traitors Ireland and how Irish designers are having their moment. Oran Aurelio is "still on the most insane high ever" after a momentous weekend in his career: designing CMAT's jaw-dropping stage outfit for her electrifying Electric Picnic appearance, and seeing his reworked designs on the premiere of season two of The Traitors Ireland. stories.title: SIPTU votes for public-sector strike action over pay
stories.summary: SIPTU members in the public sector have voted overwhelmingly in favour of industrial action, up to and including strike action. The union has accused the Government of failing to present serious proposals on pay or provide guarantees against outsourcing. The overall result among SIPTU members employed in health, local government and State agencies, who were balloted in this phase, was 97% in favour of strike action and 98% for industrial action. The previous public sector pay deal expired on 30 June, and formal talks have yet to begin on a successor agreement. Similar ballots have been announced by other public sector unions. Last week, Unite and the Prison Officers Association said their members in the public sector had voted overwhelmingly in favour of industrial action.

stories.title: Tánaiste to meet G20 finance ministers in US
stories.summary: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris will meet G20 finance ministers in the US as part of Ireland's ongoing EU presidency role. The two-day trip in North Carolina will include meetings with Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey and Canada's Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne. The event sees finance ministers and Central Bank governors from the G20 nations meet to discuss the global economy, with additional interest this week on individual countries' energy security and financial stability. As part of Ireland's EU presidency role, Mr Harris is attending alongside European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde and EU Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis. Meanwhile, further EU presidency meetings will take place in Ireland this week involving defence and foreign ministers from EU member states. This evening, defence ministers from 17 EU member states will arrive in Ireland for an informal summit chaired by Minister for Foreign Affairs and Defence Helen McEntee.

TDs backed Government plans to defer the increases, which had been planned for September and October, by 104 votes to 49. stories.title: What data tells us about emerging trends in jobs, work and wages
stories.summary: Analysis: Changing work patterns, labour supply and demographics are all shaping the Irish labour market and workplace Steven Lucas is a Senior Statistician in the Central Statistics Office (CSO), and he explains what their data can tell us about employment trends in Ireland. The official estimate of employment is drawn from the Labour Force Survey, where 32,500 households across the country are sampled every three months. Data from this survey allows us to ask different types of households detailed questions on specific elements of the labour market, such as hours worked, type of employment, availability for work, or illness or disability status, which might not be readily available from other data sources. The CSO also harnesses alternative administrative data sources, gathered by other public service bodies and adopted by the CSO for statistical purposes, to provide a timely and accurate picture of the labour market at any given time. Taken together, the CSO's ability to combine administrative and survey data securely and confidentially means we can provide a more complete picture of the labour market in Ireland than any other agency and provide insights on trends over time. Overall, Ireland has seen record levels of employment and low unemployment since the pandemic, but more recent figures show that growth has become more subdued. Our employment rate reached 75.3% in Q3 2024, which was the highest level in the series since 1998. It eased to 74.3% by Q2 2026, although the 2.84 million in employment during that quarter was still the highest level reported in the State. Over that time, the unemployment rate rose to 5.1% from 4.8% in 2025. While the labour market is strong by historical standards, it is important to continually monitor the core indicators for emerging trends.

stories.title: Spain rules out Morocco role in Ceuta migrant surge
stories.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said a rush of migrants to the enclave of Ceuta a month ago was still under investigation, while denouncing "fake information" spread by the "ultra-right". At least 70,000 people crossed into Spain's North African territory from Morocco over several days in July, triggering a Europe-wide migrant alert. Although the vast majority returned to Morocco within hours, thousands remain in the territory, many living rough on the streets. "After July 30 and 31, rumours and disinformation spread on social networks linked to Russia and Israel, and to an ultra-right international that always uses migration to attack both Spain and Europe and divide it," Mr Sánchez told Cadena Ser radio. He said it was "evident" that the two countries had used the crisis to criticise the Spanish government, as they were at odds with Madrid over its position on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Mr Sánchez was citing research by the European Union's foreign service EEAS.

stories.title: Smyth to return to New Orleans Saints practice squad
stories.summary: Charlie Smyth will remain a New Orleans Saints player and will take his place in the team's practice squad, after being waived just before the start of the new NFL season. Saints had released former Down Gaelic footballer Smyth following a competitive training camp and a final pre-season game against the Dallas Cowboys. Smyth could have join another side NFL with a deadline of 5pm on Monday (31 August) for teams to sign released players. However no other team picked him up and he will now return to the Saints practice squad. stories.title: Fourmilewater chasing glory to add to the history book
stories.summary: Championship final day is not a rare thing in Ballymacarbry, it's the norm really. When Comeragh Rangers won the 2024 Waterford Ladies SFC final, it ended the greatest winning run in Gaelic Games history with Ballymacarbry winning 42 titles in a row before that. The Nire too have brought senior football titles back to the village, 11 in all since 1993 with eight final losses bringing the appearance record to over 20 in that spell. But hurling? Hurling has had to play second fiddle to who have given their life to the Nire-Fourmilewater GAA and Ballymacarbry LGFA club on the Waterford-Tipperary border. Until now that is, because in its centenary year, Fourmile have reached the Waterford SHC final for the first time in their history with Ballygunner, the heaviest of heavyweights, awaiting in Dungarvan this afternoon. If you want evidence to back that claim up then look no further than the draw for the championship with Ballygunner having an A and B team in the senior pots. The B team, as it happens, managed 3-11 against Fourmilewater in the group stage but were still well short at the final whistle.

stories.title: European wrap: Real maintain strong start under Mourinho
stories.summary: Jude Bellingham's fine strike set Real Madrid on their way to a 4-0 La Liga rout of Malaga that gave Jose Mourinho his third win since returning to the club this summer. Bellingham beat three defenders before firing past Malaga goalkeeper Alfonso Herrero to open the scoring, and it was his header which then went in off Herrero, credited as an own goal, to make it 2-0. Trent Alexander-Arnold then set up Kylian Mbappe to make it 3-0 with half an hour gone, and Arda Guler added a late fourth. Inter Milan made it two wins from two to start the defence of their Serie A title but had to hang on for a 1-0 win at Cagliari after squandering a string of chances. Hakan Calhanoglu scored with their first real opportunity of the night 10 minutes in, but despite having a total of 30 attempts at goal on the night, Inter could not add to that and finished the night under pressure. Lazio also got their second win as Davide Frattesi’s 26th-minute strike earned a 1-0 win over Genoa, but Napoli were beaten 2-1 by Cesc Fabregas’ Como.

stories.title: Who are pop idols Katseye and why have 2 of them gone on hiatus?
stories.summary: Freelance journalist and broadcaster, writing about music and the arts. One of the most sought-after event tickets this summer has not been for the All-Ireland final, Katie Taylor's Croke Park retirement fight or the long sold-out Electric Picnic, but for the debut Irish performance by Katseye - the latest pop phenomenon to sweep the globe. Irish parents’ WhatsApp groups have descended into panicked meltdowns in search of tickets for the girl group’s gig in Dublin on September 1st, when they will kick off their 'WildWorld’ tour at the 3Arena. Tickets were snapped up within minutes of going on sale back in May: girl groups, as we’ve learned from the popularity of Blackpink, Twice, FLO, Girlset and Say Now, are big business in 2026. It’s akin to Beliebers, Directioners or Lady Gaga’s Little Monsters; Gen Z music fans may recognise elements of the aforementioned Blinks (Blackpink), Swifties (Taylor Swift) or BTS (Army) in the mania surrounding the pop band, whose fans are known as Eyekons. The Los Angeles-based six-piece have become a phenomenon since their formation in 2023, when they were drawn together via an online X Factor-style reality show called Dream Academy (a Netflix documentary about the year-long process was released in 2024). The show, which was launched on YouTube and Weverse, the South Korean fan community platform, was a collaboration between South Korean record label Hybe (the conglomerate behind the unparalleled success of K-Pop boyband BTS) and Geffen Records. The goal? Create a K-Pop-oriented pop group with a Western production style. That collusion has proven a savvy business move. The nationalities amongst Katseye’s six members - whittled down from 120,000 applicants - include Filipino, South Korean, Swiss and American, making them a truly ‘global girl group’ with an appeal across various different markets. Their management have wasted no time in positioning Daniela Avanzini, Lara Raj, Manon Bannerman, Megan Skiendiel, Sophia Laforteza and Yoonchae Jeung as the preeminent girl group for Gen Z and Gen Alpha; after all, not every band has a ‘Creative Director’ at their disposal (fashion designer Humberto Leon). The visual element has been imperative to their rise; alongside super-slick music videos accompanying their releases, there have already been collaborations with Fendi, and some notable product placement for brands like Tic Tacs and Tru Fru. Chocolate-covered fruit has suddenly never been so hip. Dismiss Katseye as a fluffy manufactured band at your peril, however: not only have their songs conquered charts around the world, but they’ve been praised by credible outlets like NME, The Guardian and The FADER and have even notched up a couple of Grammy nominations in their relatively short time together. They have played the Coachella and Lollapalooza festivals, and there has been a notable progression in their sound, too; while early songs like Touch and Debut are reasonably inoffensive pop tunes, more recent tracks like Gnarly, Pinky Up and Hootie Frutti suggest a move towards a more grown-up, daring and slightly risqué sound.

stories.title: Waxing, tweezing, shaving: When did we start removing our hair?
stories.summary: As with all fashion and beauty trends, there is a pattern when it comes to hair removal, whether it be skinny eyebrows or full armpits. "If somebody can make money from a product that's being pushed towards hair removal or hair growth, that's where the market is going to go," says Laura. A clear example is the transition from skinny 90s eyebrows to the full brows of the 2010s, and the bleached brows of today. "Brow gels were everywhere, brow laminations were everywhere," she explains. "Now they're getting smaller again because the fashion is shifting." "I think that's probably to create and allow more expression through make-up, so because of that, you've got dermaplaning becoming a big thing, so you can do that at home. Micro-needling, micro-blading - all these procedures are coming to the fore when you have that shift." Far from being a recent fad, Fitzachary explains that hair removal has a long and storied history.

stories.title: Number of doctors working in Ireland rising - reports
stories.summary: The number of doctors working in Ireland is continuing to rise with more than 22,000 now practicing here, according to a new report by the Medical Council. However, doctors are working in a health care service facing growing demand as Ireland's population continues to grow. The Medical Workforce Intelligence report 2025 found a growing, diverse workforce with a growing reliance on internationally trained doctors. The most common countries of qualification for graduates were Pakistan and Sudan. The number of female doctors has risen in recent years to just over 47%. More than a quarter of doctors reported persistent barriers to safe patient care, including pressure on workloads, time spent on bureaucracy and overcrowding.

stories.title: Forum recommends tackling energy costs for businesses
stories.summary: Energy has been identified as the principal contributor to rising business costs by an advisory forum established by the Government. The Cost of Business Advisory Forum has issued its final report setting out 63 recommendations to boost competitiveness and cut costs. The report found that the Government should consider the feasibility of a new scheme to reduce prices for large energy intensive business users. It also highlighted the importance of price transparency and easier switching for non-domestic customers. The forum brought together business representative bodies, social partners, regulators, State agencies and Government departments. Members were tasked with examining key non-pay cost drivers affecting enterprise, including energy, insurance, legal services, water and wastewater services, infrastructure and planning, tax administration and regulatory compliance, and banking and financial services.

stories.title: More cars using Dublin Port Tunnel to dodge bad traffic
stories.summary: Motorists are paying out more than €2.3m a month to dodge rush hour traffic by using the Port Tunnel in Dublin. Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) figures show a steady rise in the volume of private cars using the tunnel. In January, the transport operator increased the toll that applies to traffic headed towards the city centre from €13 to €14 while leaving the outbound toll at €12. Despite the increase, overall private car use of the Dublin Port Tunnel has continued to rise. Last year, the average number of private cars using the tunnel was 454,000. In the first six months of this year, that figure rose to 466,000, according to records released under Freedom of Inflation. During January and February - the first two months after the price rise - revenue from tolls was €2.146m and €2.143m respectively.

stories.title: O'Brien better off biding his time at Everton - Cawley
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland defender O'Brien has languished on the bench as an unused sub in the Toffees' first three games of the season, including against Preston North End in the Carabao Cup last week. It has thrown the Corkman's future on the blue half of Merseyside into serious doubt with manager David Moyes appearing to freeze him out for now. O'Brien spent much of last season playing out of position at right back - to good effect more often than not - rather than his more favoured centre-half berth. Moyes did not address the 25-year-old's future directly during a press conference on Friday. But he did appear to make a pointed message in emphasising how German midfielder Merlin Rohl has shown enthusiasm in filling in at right back without questioning the demands of the position. "Taking on the manager, he's not going to win basically," he said.

stories.title: Tribe veteran on rewarding journey to ultimate glory
stories.summary: A few weeks have now passed since their nail-biting win over Kerry at Croke Park, but Galway's All-Ireland success still feels like a deeply satisfying one for experienced defender Sarah Ní Loingsigh. A senior panellist since 2011, the Naomh Anna Leitir Mór stalwart lined out at full-back when the Tribeswomen collected the Brendan Martin Cup for just the second time in their history with a tense 2-07 to 0-12 showpiece victory at the expense of the Kingdom. The Connacht side had been pushing hard in the latter stages of the championship in recent seasons and their 2026 campaign saw them taking the final step on their journey back to the top of ladies football. This led to scenes of immense joy in the minutes that followed their one-point triumph at the Jones’ Road venue and this mood was maintained upon the squad’s return home to the west a day later. "It was amazing to see family and friends after the game and all the Galway supporters were just so happy and so emotional. It just meant so much to everyone up there and then the homecoming in Tuam the next day was just unbelievable. The scenes and the amount of fans that came out," Ní Loingsigh recalled. "Everyone was just over the moon for the group and the county. It has been a while coming. 22 years since Galway first won an All-Ireland senior title, so it was just such a relief and everyone was so proud of the group. It was lovely seeing how happy everyone was for the team as well."
